summary: Wooden tower lit 1902 on Pointe Échouerie, moved to Bonaventure point in 1907, dark since 1998; now a town-park heritage tower on the Bonaventure River, beside seasonal range lights.

light.characteristic: fixed white, 1902 to about 1910; occulting white, 15 s on and 5 s off, from about 1910 (dates per the Marine report and LighthouseFriends)
light.note: The focal height is for the 1902 site, 52 ft above high water. The tower has been dark since 1998.

structures.note: 34 ft (10 m) to the ventilator at the 1902 site; moved in 1907 and again in 2005. Octagonal iron lantern, painted red (1902 report); metal siding from 1976.

access.note: Grounds open; tower open to visitors in season (Rowlett); LighthouseFriends gives typical climbing hours 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

events.note: Lit 15 October 1902 on Pointe Échouerie (Marine report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1902, written December 1902). Built by day labour at $1,667.73.
Moved about 2 km south-west to Bonaventure point in spring 1907 (LighthouseFriends); the Marine report for the year ended 31 March 1908 records the move and its $440 cost
Fixed white changed to occulting white, 15 s visible and 5 s eclipsed, fifth-order apparatus. LighthouseFriends dates it to 1910; the Marine report is for the year ended 31 March 1911.
31 October 1965: atomizing oil burner replaced by an automated electric light; no keeper needed
Cedar shingles covered with metal siding
Recognized federal heritage building (LighthouseFriends). The Canadian Register statement (11217) does not give the date.
Moved 4.3 km to a town-owned park, beach and campground on the west side of the Bonaventure River

keepers.note: LighthouseFriends: 'at least 1914'; had been keeper at Point Échouerie before the move

keepers.name: Theodore Babin
keepers.note: Last keeper; the light was automated on 31 October 1965

corrections.proposed: inactive (the 1902 tower, dark since 1998); the active lights at the site are the seasonal Coast Guard range lights
corrections.why: The record's active status and range_lights kind describe the Coast Guard range lights, not the 1902 heritage tower.
4.6 m is the Coast Guard front range light; the heritage tower is 34 ft (10 m). The range light should be listed as a separate structure.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends and Rowlett say the 1902 tower has been dark since 1998. The Coast Guard list shows active seasonal range lights on the same shore. Both are true of different structures, and the story treats them separately.
The Marine report for the year ended 31 March 1911 records the change to occulting light; LighthouseFriends dates it to 1910. The story gives the report's year and notes LighthouseFriends' date.
The heritage record and Rowlett give 1907, LighthouseFriends says spring 1907, and the Marine report for the year ended 31 March 1908 records the move and cost. These agree.

notes_for_editor: Read: Marine annual reports for the years ended 30 June 1902, 31 March 1908 and 31 March 1911 (all in the local corpus, scan pages checked with corpus.py page), LighthouseFriends, Canadian Register 11217, Rowlett, the Coast Guard list of lights (Chaleur Bay), and the RPCQ Cap-Alright record for disambiguation. The French Wikipedia article was read for leads only and is not cited (it gives the 2 km and spring 1907 move, 'Pointe Souris', and the 2005 move; all of these are covered by cited sources). Status conflict: the station record lists the place as active range_lights, but the old tower has been dark since 1998 (LighthouseFriends, Rowlett); the Coast Guard range lights (1369, 1369.1) are separate seasonal aids. The station record's coordinates (48.035674, -65.482807) and the Coast Guard front range (48 02 09.3 N, 065 28 56.8 W) and the LighthouseFriends tower coordinates are within about 40 m of each other, so the tower and the range lights share a site; the story does not say how far apart they stand. The 1902 focal height (52 ft above high water) is for the 1902 site; no figure is given for the 1907 site. The 1902 range (12 miles) is in the report's unit, which it does not give as nautical; the story says so. Keepers: all names come from LighthouseFriends. The Marine lists for 1907 to 1911 print a Quebec keeper table in separate columns, and 'Echouerie' could not be matched to a keeper by position with any confidence, so no Marine citation is given for the keepers. The Captain O'Farelle complaint (1906) is attributed to LighthouseFriends; a search of the 1906 Marine report for 'Farrell', 'Farelle' and 'Echouerie' did not find it. A Marine note of the steamer Otranto stranding 'at Bonaventure' on 26 November 1908 is in the report for the year ended 31 March 1909; the report does not tie it to the light, so it is not listed as a wreck here. Canadian lens orders: 7th (1902 and 1908 report) and 5th (1911 report and LighthouseFriends). Fact-check 2026-10-27: the Marine scan pages were confirmed against the OCR page index (1902 report scan p. 79, 1908 scan p. 81, 1911 scan p. 78); no name was matched by column position, so no page image was needed. Rowlett gives the present tower as 7.5 m (25 ft) square pyramidal wood (the story gives the 1902 measure of 10 m to the ventilator only). The story has five chapters against the Moderate range of two to four; the editor should decide whether to merge chapters.
